## 1. The error report promises less than it sends

**What the person sees.** The "Something went wrong on our side" dialog says
the report is only the lines shown: "That is the whole report. It has no chat
messages, no files, no project names and no account or email address."
Preferences › Updates › Error reports says the same and adds "JusPrin's server
sees your IP address, as with any web page."

**What is actually sent.** Since a14e9d762f (reports go straight to Sentry)
every report also carries this run's log file
(`Support/SentryClient.cpp:159-166`), the native stack, the loaded modules
and the machine. The home folder is no longer replaced by "~", and the report
goes to Sentry, not JusPrin's server. For the app's own reports the dialog's
"Where" row is empty, so it says "That is the whole report" while a stack and
the log go with it. The log can name project files and folders.

**Where.** `Shell/ErrorReportDialog.cpp:116-117, 141-143, 225-234`,
`AgentUI/src/components/Preferences.tsx:657`.

**Needs Kenneth.** This is a wording decision or a decision about what to
send, not a code fix alone. His earlier "Keep the promise and accept the
risk" (b3eed3bf4b) was about error text, before the log was attached. Bring
him the choice: make the sentences say what is sent (new wording, translated
into the 22 languages), or send less (no log file, home folder trimmed again,
which he had removed: "delete both older trims"). Do not pick for him.
Before writing any sentence that says what a report never holds, check what
the log file can contain.

## 2. An AI reply can spin forever

**What the person sees.** The reply spinner never stops, and the chat stays
busy until they press Stop. With automatic reports on, no dialog opens, so
nothing tells them anything.

**Cause found by reading.** Only `pump_stream`'s handler
(`Agent/AgentHost.cpp:3442`) ends a reply as failed. Two other paths can
throw without ending it:
- starting the request: `begin_stream` calls `m_agent->start` at
  `AgentHost.cpp:3034`, which can throw from `post()`
  (`ProviderAgent.cpp:462`) or from `keep_blob`'s write;
- continuing after a tool result: `continue_after_tool`
  (`AgentHost.cpp:3410`) can throw from `next_call` (`ProviderAgent.cpp:585`)
  or its `post()`.

The throw reaches the page-message handler or the shell timer's
`reported(...)`, is reported under the wrong "was doing", and `fail_stream`
never runs, so `m_stream` stays set.

## 3. A printer card on Home can freeze for the rest of the run

**What the person sees.** One printer's card on Home stops updating and shows
its last reading until the app restarts. Quitting waits 3 seconds.

**Cause found by reading.** `Printers/HostLaneReader.cpp:213-216` wraps the
read thread in `reported()`. If `read()` throws, `shared->finish(...)` and
`--running` are skipped. The printer stays marked in flight, so `begin()`
never reads it again this run. The failure is reported once.

## 4. The printer chat can stay on "Checking <address>"

paid ai check can use claude subscription, right? If so, tell the session to do so

No, it can't. The paid check exists to test the model the app ships with by default, `gpt-5.4-mini` from OpenAI, and your Claude subscription only runs Claude models. The free run on your subscription has already happened: the session ran both prompt suites through it.

The testing notes in `tests/project_prompt/README.md` explain why that free run isn't enough. A stronger model can cover over an unclear prompt that the weaker default trips on, so a pass on a Claude model doesn't show that `gpt-5.4-mini` will pass. Running the paid check "on the subscription" would just repeat the free run.

So I haven't messaged the session. The choice is still yours: spend about $1–3 on the OpenAI run, or skip it for 2.0.1.
what's the purpose of this test?

The test checks that the AI still behaves correctly in the app's chats. It covers the instructions the app sends the model, the tool descriptions and the skills, and it runs on the model most people will actually get.

The app has saved test cases. Each one is a recorded situation, such as someone saying "I want to print this", or a Klipper printer that has shut down. The test sends that situation to a real model and has a second model judge the reply. The judge checks things like: did the AI call the right tool, and did it say the printer can't print until Klipper restarts? Each case runs a few times, and the pass count is compared with saved results from earlier.

You need it before a release because a change to the prompts, skills or tool text can make the AI worse without any normal test failing. Unit tests check the code, not what the model does with the words.

The paid run uses `gpt-5.4-mini` because it's the app's default model, and a weaker model trips over unclear wording that Claude works around. The free run on your subscription used Claude. A pass there shows the prompts work for a strong model, not for the one most people get.

For 2.0.1 the free run already found three cases that sometimes fail. The session ran them again on 2.0.0 and got about the same results, so this release didn't cause them. The paid run would tell you whether `gpt-5.4-mini` does as well as Claude on this release's prompts. That matters most here because this release changed AI instructions, including removing the rule that made the AI keep checking a slice it had started.
So it's just a smoke testing to make sure the clouds worked as we expected? If it's a smoke testing, why would it cost a lot more than the prompt testing, which is supposed to be a lot more thorough?

No, it isn't a smoke test, and it isn't more expensive work. It's the same prompt test, run on a different model.

- **The free run** sent the test cases to Claude through your Claude subscription. The subscription charges nothing per request, so it shows as $0. The work still costs something: it uses up some of your subscription's usage limits, which you share with your own Claude Code work.
- **The paid run** sends the same cases, or a smaller set of them, to OpenAI's `gpt-5.4-mini` through the API. OpenAI bills that per token, so it shows up as real money.

So the price difference isn't about how thorough each run is. One goes through a flat-fee subscription, and the other goes through a pay-per-use API. $1–3 is also small. It's what a few dozen chats with long prompts cost on a cheap model. The session said a comparable batch last time cost about $0.50.

The reason to run it at all is the model. The free run shows the prompts work on Claude. The paid run shows they work on the model the app actually ships with as its default, which is weaker and trips more easily over unclear wording.
If what's the purpose of doing the paid run if assuming that we have already done the free run?

The paid run would catch one thing the free run can't: a prompt change that a weaker model gets wrong while Claude handles it fine. Claude often guesses what an unclear instruction meant. A cheaper model follows it literally, or ignores it. So the free run can pass while people on the default model see the AI misbehave.

For 2.0.1 that's the only thing it would add. The free run already compared this release with 2.0.0 on the cases that failed, and they came out about the same.

I'm also not sure the paid run tests the right model, and I haven't checked this:
- The testing notes call `gpt-5.4-mini` the app's default, but it's the default only for someone who uses their own OpenAI key.
- People who use AI through a JusPrin account go through JusPrin's server, which picks the model itself. My notes from earlier work say that's DeepSeek V4 Flash, not `gpt-5.4-mini`.

If most people use a JusPrin account, the paid run tests a model few of them get.

My pick is to skip it for 2.0.1:

- The paid run's model may not be the one most people use.

If you want a check on a weaker model, the better target is the model the JusPrin account actually serves, once I've confirmed which one that is.
